description: The CIA triad, and how developers think about threats before code ships.

screens.body:
You don't need a security degree to write safer code. Most breaches start as ordinary bugs — a missing check, an input nobody questioned.

Think of security as quality with consequences. A crash annoys a user; a security bug can expose their messages, photos, or money.

The good news: a handful of habits — this topic's whole job — stop the majority of attacks.

options: Most breaches start as ordinary coding bugs
Only security experts ever touch code
Security is handled by firewalls alone
check.question: Why should every dev learn basic security?

screens.heading: Security is a dev job
screens.keyPoint: Security = quality with consequences. Small habits stop most attacks.

screens.body:
Confidentiality means the right eyes only. Your DMs, grades, medical notes — seen by you and the people you chose, nobody else.

Devs protect it with login walls, access rules ("only the owner can read this"), and encryption that scrambles data for everyone else.

Quick test: if this data appeared on a billboard, who would be hurt? That tells you how much protection it needs.

check.question: A user's private messages leak. Which pillar broke?

screens.heading: C is for Confidentiality
screens.keyPoint: Confidentiality = only the right people can see it.

screens.body:
Integrity means data stays correct and untampered. Your bank balance reads what it should — nobody quietly edited it.

Attackers love silent changes: tweak a price from $100 to $1, or flip an "unpaid" invoice to "paid".

Devs protect integrity with validation ("this value must make sense"), permissions ("only admins can edit prices"), and checks that detect tampering.

check.question: Someone secretly changes a product price from $100 to $1. Which pillar broke?

screens.heading: I is for Integrity

screens.body:
Availability means the system works when people need it. Your study app opens during exam week. The store checkout works on payday.

Attacks like DDoS flood a site with junk traffic until real users can't get in. But ordinary bugs — a crash loop, a full disk — break availability too.

Devs protect it with rate limits, backups, and handling errors so one failure doesn't take everything down.

check.question: A flood of junk traffic knocks a site offline. Which pillar broke?

screens.heading: A is for Availability
screens.keyPoint: Availability = it works when people need it.

screens.body:
Threat modeling sounds fancy — it's just asking "what could go wrong?" before it does.

Step one: list your crown jewels. Passwords, payment details, private messages, session tokens — the things that would hurt most if stolen, changed, or lost.

You can't protect everything equally, so you rank: guard the crown jewels hardest.

options: List what's most valuable if stolen or lost
check.question: What's the first step of threat modeling?

screens.heading: Threat modeling, step 1: name what's valuable
screens.keyPoint: List your crown jewels first — protect those hardest.

screens.body:
Step two: find every door into your system. A "door" is anywhere untrusted data enters — forms, URL parameters, file uploads, APIs, even copy-pasted text.

Security people call these trust boundaries: the line between "their input" and "your system". Everything crossing that line gets checked.

Sketch your app and mark each door. Most attacks walk through a door someone forgot.

options: The line where untrusted input enters your system
The edge of your Wi-Fi range
check.question: What's a trust boundary?

screens.heading: Threat modeling, step 2: name the doors
screens.keyPoint: Every input is a door. Find them all, check them all.

screens.body:
One lock can be picked. Five locks means an attacker must beat all five — and you'll probably notice.

That's defense in depth: validation AND access checks AND logging AND rate limits, stacked together.

If one layer fails (a bug slips past validation), the next layer catches it. Never bet everything on a single check.

options: So one failed layer doesn't mean total failure
It makes the code run faster
check.question: Why stack multiple security layers?

screens.heading: Defense in depth: layers, not one lock
screens.keyPoint: Stack layers so one failure isn't fatal.

screens.body:
The security world has amazing free references — these three are the classics:

• OWASP Top 10 — the ten most common web app risks, updated regularly: https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/
• OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — short, practical "how to do it right" guides: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/
• OWASP ASVS — the full checklist for verifying app security: https://owasp.org/www-project-application-security-verification-standard/
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: OWASP is the free, trusted library of app security — bookmark it.
